title: Expert Systems in Law: A Jurisprudential Approach to Artificial Intelligence and Legal Reasoning
author: Richard E. Susskind

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Expert systems: Retrieval differs from replacing judgment
st.an: Susskind accepts the distinction between retrieval and expert legal assistance, then materially develops it into a jurisprudential design programme: systems should make their theories of law explicit, capture specialist heuristics, address fact selection and indeterminacy, and provide authority-based explanations. His qualified feasibility claims also reinforce the synthesis’s caution that prototypes did not yet establish practical utility or replacement of legal judgment.
qs: The former systems are designed to function as non-intelligent supportive components in the general legal problem-solving process, while the latter (which may embody or interface with the former), assist in the more specific interpretative processes requiring a level of knowledge normally associated only with intelligent human beings.

It is beyond argument, however, that all expert systems must conform to some jurisprudential theory because all expert systems in law necessarily make assumptions about the nature of law and legal reasoning.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source supports selective, expertise-led deployment by arguing that legal AI is restricted by open texture, non-deductive fact classification and shallow representations of legal judgment. It materially extends the cluster by prescribing intensive treatment of bounded domains, jurisprudentially grounded knowledge representation, expert consultation and transparent explanations supported by legal authority.
qs: Perhaps the most telling objection to deduction in law with regard to all the projects is what can be termed The Argument from Particularity of Facts.73 This asserts that the crucial, and non- deductive, stage in legal reasoning is that of classifying the particular facts of the case, a stage in which none of the current computer systems are of support.
For in accordance with that analysis, there seems little doubt that intensive coverage of a small legal domain is preferable to superficial coverage of an extensive area of law.

st.t: Executable rules: Formalisation conceals interpretive choices
st.an: Susskind supports the cluster’s central distinction between executable rules and fuller legal expertise. He identifies fact classification as a crucial non-deductive limitation, treats operational utility as unproven, and favours narrow, expert-informed systems that assist practitioners and provide legally substantive explanations.
qs: Perhaps the most telling objection to deduction in law with regard to all the projects is what can be termed The Argument from Particularity of Facts.73 This asserts that the crucial, and non- deductive, stage in legal reasoning is that of classifying the particular facts of the case, a stage in which none of the current computer systems are of support.

If a system is to replicate a human expert in law, it ought to provide more penetrating explanations than these, by clarifying the rules and, as Bellord realises, also by stating legal authorities for all material propositions advanced.

kp.k: Retrieval systems differ fundamentally from legal problem-solving systems
kp.d: Susskind distinguishes document databases such as LEXIS from knowledge-based systems that assist with interpretation and problem-solving. He reports criticisms that keyword relevance produces irrelevant results or misses relevant documents, while acknowledging that poor search formulation can explain some deficiencies. A separate motivation for expert systems is practitioners’ need for experiential know-how rather than simply access to primary sources.
qs: The occurrence of the keyword(s) in the full text (or head notes) of documents, therefore, is the determinative factor with regard to the relevance, or otherwise, of the data retrieved.

The former systems are designed to function as non-intelligent supportive components in the general legal problem-solving process, while the latter (which may embody or interface with the former), assist in the more specific interpretative processes requiring a level of knowledge normally associated only with intelligent human beings.

kp.k: Expert systems would assist general practitioners with specialist problems
kp.d: The proposed service model is assistance to general practitioners confronting matters beyond their expertise, potentially reducing their need to consult human specialists on every such occasion. Systems would guide users through questions and apply specialists’ formal and experiential knowledge; teaching is another envisaged use. This is a proposed capability, not an account of established deployment.
qs: These expert systems are designed to function as intelligent assistants in the process of legal problem- solving (and can also be used as teaching aids).

The users of such systems are intended to be general legal practitioners, who, when faced with legal problems beyond their range of experience and knowledge, rather than always having to turn to appropriately qualified legal specialists, may instead consult their expert systems in law.

kp.k: Expertise requires depth, explanations, and maintainable knowledge
kp.d: Susskind reserves the designation expert system for systems developed with human experts and capable of expert-level performance in specialised domains. He identifies transparency, heuristic knowledge and flexibility as essential attributes, favouring intensive coverage of narrow domains over superficial breadth. His criticism of E.L.I. concerns its lack of explanations and expert heuristics, not a denial of its technical significance.
qs: Expert systems are usually: (1) transparent, which means that they can generate explanations of the lines of reasoning that lead them to their conclusions;
there seems little doubt that intensive coverage of a small legal domain is preferable to superficial coverage of an extensive area of law.
More importantly, E.L.I. does not reason with legal experts’ heuristic knowledge.

kp.k: Preserving specialist knowledge could mitigate dependence on individuals
kp.d: Susskind predicts that expert systems could help the profession manage increasing specialisation driven partly by expanding statutes and reported cases. He presents the departure of experienced practitioners, scholars and judges as a threat to continuity of expertise, and suggests that systems could preserve and distribute that knowledge indefinitely. The possibility of assistance exceeding an individual expert’s quality is explicitly speculative.
qs: It may now be possible, however, by use of expert systems in law, to preserve indefinitely, and to put at the disposal of others, the wealth of legal knowledge and expertise of various experts, hitherto bestowed upon the legal world in transient and indiscriminate doses.
More than this, a “law machine” may now be able to offer assistance of a quality possibly greater than that of any one individual human legal expert.

kp.k: Operational legal expert systems remained unrealised in 1986
kp.d: Reviewing research following Buchanan and Headrick’s 1970 paper, Susskind reports no more than 25 sustained projects and no fully operational legal expert system useful to the profession. He nevertheless judges limited-scope construction technically feasible. His survey distinguishes prototypes and research models from usable professional products; for example, LDS models civil settlement decision-making rather than functioning as a completed legal reasoning assistant.
qs: Since then, no more than 25 sustained research projects have been launched in this field,
there has not yet been developed a fully operational expert system in law that is of utility to the legal profession.
Indeed we can now reasonably assert, in terms of the necessary computational tools, such an enterprise (at least of limited scope), is technically feasible.

kp.k: Cross-domain successes motivate, but do not establish, legal feasibility
kp.d: Susskind reports achievements in chemistry, geology and medical diagnosis as motivations for legal expert systems, often qualifying performance reports as claims. He contrasts natural-science systems grounded in descriptive causal laws with legal reasoning involving prescriptive laws and formal legal sources. He treats this distinction as an insufficiently examined possible explanation for law’s slower progress, rather than a demonstrated causal finding.
qs: The system’s capabilities in this sphere are now said to exceed those of any single human being (including its designers), and it is used in university and industrial environments throughout the world.

As a direct result of its advice (its knowledge base contains the heuristic and formal knowledge of scientists of the U.S. Geological Survey), it is claimed that a molybdenum find, valued at one hundred million dollars, was rnade in 1982.

kp.k: Jurisprudence should guide legal system design
kp.d: The central recommendation is to use legal theory to specify models of law and reasoning before computational implementation. Susskind argues that every legal expert system necessarily embodies jurisprudential assumptions, whether acknowledged or not. He proposes seeking agreement among theories on straightforward matters and, where agreement fails, developing models that conflict as little as possible with prevailing theories.
qs: all expert systems in law necessarily make assumptions about the nature of law and legal reasoning.
If there is not, and if these conflicts affect the expert system enterprise, then a model that clashes as little as possible with the ruling theories should be developed.

kp.k: Acquiring and representing expertise require substantive legal interpretation
kp.d: Susskind finds little heuristic content in existing systems, which usually restructure statutory material and give case law less attention. He treats knowledge representation as the central legal knowledge-engineering issue: unlike storing documents, it requires interpreting, individuating and restructuring law while preserving meaning. He recommends drawing on jurisprudence rather than forcing legal material into a preferred programming language.
qs: In general, the systems that have been developed to date have minimal heuristic content and no methods have yet been suggested that might eliminate this deficit.
The knowledge represented in the systems usually consists of restructured statutory source material (case law has received far less treatment)
The legal data is not interpreted for this purpose, but is simply fed into the computer as the raw material of the process of legal reasoning.

kp.k: Deductive reasoning faces conditional jurisprudential limits
kp.d: Susskind characterises leading systems as predominantly deductive and examines objections concerning normative truth values and open-textured language. If deontic logic is the only satisfactory answer to the truth-value objection, he argues, inference engines would need it. Accepting Hart’s analysis would restrict solely deductive systems to clear cases rather than borderline disputes. These are conditional theoretical arguments, not measured system-performance findings.
qs: Because legal norms lack truth value, it is argued, they cannot be related to the facts of case by the logic of theoretical reasoning, that is, reasoning about what is the case.
inference procedures are solely deductive will function exclusively in the clear case domain, and will be of no aid in the solving of “problems of the penumbra.”

kp.k: Fact classification determines whether automation offers practical value
kp.d: Susskind argues that selecting and classifying operative facts is a crucial non-deductive component of legal work that existing systems do not support. Applying familiar rules to supplied facts may therefore offer general practitioners little value. He proposes building in genuinely specialist domains, adding explicit heuristics and meta-rules to help select facts, or combining both approaches; his project investigates the combined option.
qs: This asserts that the crucial, and non- deductive, stage in legal reasoning is that of classifying the particular facts of the case, a stage in which none of the current computer systems are of support.
Thirdly, they must adopt the second strategy in tandem with the first, that is, develop an expert system in law that also aids in the fact finding process.

kp.k: Explanations should clarify rules and identify legal authority
kp.d: Susskind criticises explanations consisting merely of the rules triggered during computation. A system approximating legal expertise should clarify those rules and identify authorities for material propositions. He also recommends exploring interfaces with document databases so users can consult the primary sources underlying the represented knowledge.
qs: If a system is to replicate a human expert in law, it ought to provide more penetrating explanations than these, by clarifying the rules and, as Bellord realises, also by stating legal authorities for all material propositions advanced.
This could be achieved by interfacing expert systems in law with already existing database systems in law such as LEXIS.

kp.k: Different legal reasoning functions require explicit design choices
kp.d: Susskind argues that research reports insufficiently distinguish justification, persuasion, prediction and reconciliation of legal texts with values. He also identifies an unresolved possibility: using a common knowledge base with different inference engines for different kinds of users and purposes. He presents this as a research opportunity rather than an established capability.
qs: little mention is made in the research reports about whether the systems are intended to assist the user in, say, justifying a legal conclusion, persuading a given audience, predicting the ruling of a court, or in reconciling legid texts with certain values,

Indeed perhaps the most stimulating possibility in this field is that of developing a system that can be used by several classes of reasoning agent for their own very different and respective purposes.

kp.k: Oxford research proposes reusable models and a divorce-law demonstrator
kp.d: The Oxford project seeks to turn jurisprudential models into formal specifications supporting reusable legal expert-system construction, with a demonstrator in Scottish divorce law drawing on statutes and precedents. Susskind reports methods already developed for describing, individuating and structuring laws, but presents formal models, a reusable shell and the demonstrator as work in progress. He anticipates decades of research on the broader unresolved problems, including natural-language input, uncertainty, fact finding and database integration.
qs: The above eight problems will require decades of attention from the most skilful exponents in the field.
Our chosen domain belongs to Scottish Law of Divorce, whose sources are to be found both in statutes and judicial precedents.
A portion of the Scottish Legal System is particularly appropriate, as the law in that jurisdiction manifests features of both civil and common law systems.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Susskind envisages specialised legal expert systems as intelligent assistants that extend general practitioners’ access to expertise, preserve specialist knowledge, and potentially offer assistance exceeding that of an individual expert.
pts.d: Susskind predicts that general practitioners could consult expert systems for problems outside their experience rather than invariably consulting human specialists. The systems would question users, guide problem-solving, explain their reasoning and potentially supply legal authority; they could also serve as teaching aids. He argues that widespread use could alleviate difficulties caused by increasing legal specialisation and preserve expertise otherwise lost when senior practitioners, academics or judges depart. Assistance superior to that of any individual expert is presented as a possibility, not a demonstrated legal capability. He also identifies the prospective value of systems serving different classes of legal reasoning agent for different purposes. These are claims about knowledge-based expert systems, not merely document retrieval or machines possessing cognitive states.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is a qualitative review of early research systems, experience reported in other domains, legal theory and an ongoing Oxford project—not demonstrated commercial legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: Susskind surveys projects including TAXMAN, JUDITH, LDS, statutory PROLOG systems, TAXADVISOR and E.L.I. He treats their collective achievements as evidence that a limited legal expert system is computationally feasible, while explicitly stating that no fully operational system useful to the profession has yet been developed. His discussion of chemical, geological and medical expert systems supplies cross-domain precedents, with some performance accounts expressly described as reported or claimed. The Slot Report is cited for lawyers’ need for practical know-how relative to primary legal sources. His proposed benefits remain prospective: the paper offers no measured legal productivity gains, cost reductions or labour-market effects. Jurisprudential arguments support his claims about design requirements and limitations. The Oxford Scottish divorce-law system is an undertaking intended to demonstrate the approach, not a completed validation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing in 1986, Susskind sees limited technical feasibility in the present but makes practical benefits conditional on further development, with major research problems requiring decades.
pts.d: No date is given for widespread deployment. The envisioned benefits depend on successful construction and use of systems with specialised, deep knowledge acquired with legal experts’ assistance, including experiential heuristics, meaningful explanations and maintainable knowledge bases. Susskind argues that legal theory should inform knowledge representation and inference. His claim that purely deductive systems are restricted to clear cases is expressly conditional on accepting Hart’s analysis of open texture. He also argues that systems merely applying familiar rules to supplied facts risk being of little use to general practitioners: developers should work in genuinely expert domains, support identification of operative facts, or do both. Handling uncertainty and analogy, natural-language interaction and integration with primary-source databases remain research tasks. Oxford’s proposed general models and shell are aspirations rather than completed capabilities.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal intended beneficiaries are general practitioners and the profession’s users of specialist knowledge; experts, educators and system builders are also affected.
pts.d: General practitioners would gain guided assistance in unfamiliar specialised matters, with clients benefiting indirectly through their advisers. Human legal specialists would supply the expertise embodied in systems, and consultation of those systems could replace some referrals for specialist advice; Susskind does not quantify displacement or predict the elimination of specialists. Law firms, academia and the judiciary are discussed as locations where the departure of experienced individuals can remove valuable expertise. Students could benefit from teaching applications. Legal knowledge engineers, computer scientists and legal theorists are assigned interdependent roles in building systems. Susskind envisages findings relevant across legal domains and legal systems, using Scottish divorce law, with statutory and judicial sources, as the demonstration domain. He does not advance a specific prediction about firm staffing ratios, pricing, employment totals or direct public access to justice.
